<reason>A won on the motion as written. The proposition targets access tied to work status, and A's job-lock case was never squarely neutralized: B's escape route depended on a regulated individual market, statutory subsidies, and continuity rules — features that effectively concede A's design principle while drifting away from "employer-based insurance tying access to work status." A exposed this asymmetry repeatedly, and B never explained why the rules-and-subsidies governance it grants itself is unavailable to a single payer. B's best unique argument — the annual-appropriations asymmetry (cuts by inaction vs. cuts by visible vote) — was sharp and the strongest technical exchange of the debate, but A's closing answer that a public entitlement can also be set in standing law met it, and B's retort ("a single payer no real system runs") was thin and unsupported. Both sides answered pressure questions directly and honestly; A's Q2 (why do subsidies survive the same squeeze) placed pressure B only partially absorbed. B was rhetorically superior ("Job-lock deserves a patch. Monopoly deserves a veto."; "fails in pieces vs. everywhere at once") and more original on the appropriations asymmetry, but the decisive clash — dependable entitlement versus patched employment dependence — resolved in A's favor, aided by A's accurate correction of B's Switzerland example.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's Rebuttal 2 appropriations asymmetry (denying care requires a vote in a multi-payer system; funding care requires one under single payer) against A's closing response that standing statutory law can protect a public entitlement too, turning B's own reliance on durable statutory subsidies into a concession of A's principle. A's second Pressure Question set this up by exposing the double standard, and the follow-through carried the round.</best_rebuttal>
